plan.topic: Smartwatch calorie estimates off by 15–25% vs lab gold standard, with larger errors at higher body fat (PLOS One)
plan.angle: 'Your watch's calories-burned number is a rough estimate.' In a small lab test (58 adults, 10 minutes of cycling), 4 popular smartwatches were off by a median of about 15–25% against a lab gas-analysis gold standard. Most overestimated, and the error grew at higher body fat. It's a small, short study, so treat it as a caution, not a verdict. Watches are better at tracking trends in steps and heart rate than exact calories. Don't extrapolate weekly calorie totals and give no eating instructions. Suggested title: 'How Accurate Is Your Smartwatch's Calorie Count? A Lab Test Checked'.
plan.working_title: Should You Eat Back Your Apple Watch Calories? A Lab Test Says Think Twice
plan.why: Published today with almost no creator coverage and low competition. Product-specific and visual, the kind of thing that spreads on TikTok and Shorts. Doubles as a myth-buster. | fact-check: Verified: PLOS One, published 29 Jul 2026, 'Body fat, skin tone, and the accuracy of smartwatch caloric expenditure estimates' (PubMed 42525581). n=58 Hispanic adults, one 10-minute recumbent-cycling protocol, compared with indirect calorimetry (COSMED K5). Devices: Apple Watch S8, Fitbit Sense 2, Samsung GW5, Garmin FR955. Median error was ~15–25%. Apple, Garmin and Samsung overestimated, and error grew with body fat. Problems: (1) The '1,200–2,400 kcal a week' figure is our own extrapolation from a 10-minute cycling test, not a study finding. Drop it. (2) 'Eat back your calories' framing pushes calorie-restriction advice at a broad audience, which is an eating-disorder risk. Reframe it as 'treat the number as a rough estimate'. (3) State the limits: one short cycling test, one population, 58 people. Sources: https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0353261 ; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42525581/

factcheck.summary: The script is accurate and safe. The main study (Kostrna et al., PLOS One, July 2026, vol 21(7), e0353261) exists, and the script describes it correctly. It had 58 Hispanic adults with a mean age of 23. They did one 10-minute recumbent cycling session wearing the Apple Watch Series 8, Fitbit Sense 2, Samsung Galaxy Watch 5 and Garmin Forerunner 955. The benchmark was indirect calorimetry with a COSMED K5 unit. The paper says the median absolute percentage error was about 15–25%. Apple, Garmin and Samsung showed a clear positive (overestimating) bias. Fitbit showed little average bias but varied a lot. Higher body fat was linked to bigger errors, and skin tone had no significant effect. The paper names its own limits: one type of exercise, a small group with the darkest skin type, and wearing the watches at the same time. The script's caveat in s5 handles this well. The 2017 Shcherbina/Stanford paper (J Pers Med 7(2):3) supports the claim that heart rate is fairly accurate while calorie counts are not. It tested 60 adults on 7 wrist devices and found heart-rate error mostly around or below 5%, while no device got energy expenditure within 20%. Framing is careful throughout: "linked to", "in this study", and "a caution, not a verdict". The PubMed and PMC pages were blocked by a captcha when fetched directly, but search results confirmed both records exist at the listed URLs. I found only minor wording issues and no safety concerns. Calories are framed as a "ballpark", which does not encourage restrictive eating.

issues.claim: The watches were off by a median of roughly 15 to 25 percent.
issues.problem: The study measured activity calories only (PAEE: calories burned by the exercise itself), not total daily calories. As written, viewers could assume their all-day calorie total is off by the same amount, which this study did not test.
issues.fix: Replace narration with: "During the workout, the watches' calorie counts were off by a median of roughly 15 to 25 percent. The catch? Three of the four tended to overestimate."

issues.claim: On-screen text: "Your watch's calories? A guess."
issues.problem: "A guess" is stronger than both the narration ("a rough estimate") and the evidence. The watches use sensors and algorithms; they are imprecise, not random.
issues.fix: Change on_screen_text to: "Your watch's calories? An estimate."

issues.claim: Heart rate is where watches do better — lab tests show it's usually close.
issues.problem: This is supported by Shcherbina 2017 (most devices had about 5% or less heart-rate error). But those were older devices, and accuracy was lowest during walking. "Usually close" is acceptable. Tying it to lab tests of resting and steady exercise makes it more precise.
issues.fix: Replace narration with: "Heart rate is where watches do better — in lab tests it's usually within a few percent. Calories? Treat them as a ballpark, not a receipt."

audio.soundNotes: I kept the music level as is: it sits at −14 dB under the voice and in pauses, which is on target. I cut stacked duplicate transition layers and pop clusters so no second has more than 3–4 hits, and lowered the swoosh at 29.4 s and the pop at 34.2 s from about −11 and −13 dB to about −16 dB. I also removed two swells that were effectively silent at about −52 dB. I added three subtle custom sounds: a smartwatch tap at the start, a monitor pulse under 'Heart rate' and a receipt printer for 'Ballpark, not a receipt'. They're set at conservative levels.

hold_reason: Packaging check REVISE: I checked the packaging against the verified content summary only, as asked. I did not re-check the science. The YouTube title matches the verified finding and doesn't overpromise. All captions keep the main points right: a median error of about 15–25%, compared against the lab gold standard, "ballpark, not a receipt," and the extra body-fat error described as a link found in this study, not a cause. The IG and FB captions say how limited the study was (one short cycling test in young Hispanic adults). The heart-rate line fits what src3 (Shcherbina 2017) reports for most devices. Four small fixes are needed before publishing. (1) The #appleWatch hashtag suggests Apple Watch was one of the watches tested, which the verified summary doesn't confirm. (2) The Instagram line about being tempted to "eat back" your workout could read as encouraging people to eat less, which conflicts with the brand's eating-disorder rule. (3) The TikTok caption has no caveat about the study's size and no disclaimer. (4) The study details (58 adults, 10 minutes of cycling, 3 of 4 watches overestimating, young Hispanic adults) are not in the one-line verified summary I was given. They look like they came from the verified script, but someone should confirm that before this auto-publishes. I could not verify src1 and src2 myself (I had no web access in this run), so they are listed as upstream-verified. src3 is a real publication that I recognize (J Pers Med 2017;7(2):3, PMC5491979); I did not open the link in this run.; test run: review before publishing
